title: Over 100,000 Floridians May Now Hold Canadian Citizenship Under New Law
excerpt: Canada's Bill C-3 scrapped the first-generation limit on citizenship by descent, opening a path for Americans with Canadian ancestors — no test, no oath, just proof.
body:
• Canada's Bill C-3, in force since December 15, 2025, removed the first-generation limit on citizenship by descent — people born before that date with a Canadian parent, grandparent or even more distant ancestor may already be citizens.
  • US Census data shows roughly 59,000 Florida residents of Canadian ancestry and 99,000 of French Canadian ancestry — together, well over 100,000 Floridians may hold a second citizenship without knowing it.
  • Applications have surged: the US generated the most demand, with nearly 2,500 citizenship-by-descent applications in January 2026 alone, and IRCC processing times have stretched to roughly 12 months.
  • Qualifying is automatic and retroactive — no test or oath is needed — but applicants must document an unbroken chain of descent through birth and marriage records, and archives face heavy backlogs.

More than 100,000 Floridians may already be Canadian citizens — and most of them have no idea. Under Canada's Bill C-3, which came into force on December 15, 2025, the country scrapped the first-generation limit that for years blocked citizenship from passing to children born abroad when their Canadian parent was also born outside Canada. The change means anyone born before that date who can trace an unbroken line of descent to a Canadian ancestor — a grandparent, a great-grandparent, or further back — is already a citizen by operation of law.

Florida, with its deep history of Canadian migration, is ground zero for the shift in the United States. Five-year estimates from the 2024 American Community Survey show close to 59,000 Florida residents identifying Canadian ancestry and a further 99,000 identifying French Canadian ancestry. Both categories fall under the new law's descent provisions, pointing to well over 100,000 Floridians with a potential claim — a number that is likely conservative, since family history is not always well documented.

What Bill C-3 changed

Since 2009, Canadian law imposed a first-generation limit: only the first generation born outside Canada to a Canadian parent could inherit citizenship. If your parent was born in Canada, you were Canadian — but if your parent was also born outside the country, citizenship could not pass to you. The rule created a class of people known as "Lost Canadians," and Ontario courts found aspects of the limit unconstitutional in the 2023 Bjorkquist case.

Bill C-3 fixed that. For people born before December 15, 2025, there is now no generational limit on how far citizenship can pass down. There is no test or oath to pass: applicants file for proof of citizenship with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), and once approved receive a citizenship certificate confirming their status.

"If you qualify, you are already a Canadian citizen — you simply need to apply for proof of citizenship. There is no deadline to apply."

— Immigration guidance for Americans, immigration.ca

A surge in applications — and backlogs

The response has been dramatic. IRCC received more than 12,000 citizenship-by-descent applications between December 15 and the end of January, with Americans filing the largest share — nearly 2,500 in January alone, according to data reported by the Canadian Press. Across all of 2025, the department received about 82,500 such applications, with the US generating the most demand at roughly 24,500.

Processing times for citizenship certificates have stretched to approximately 12 months, up sharply from five months in mid-2025, with inventories exceeding 70,000 files. Provincial archives are under pressure too: Quebec's national archives reportedly saw a 3,000% increase in requests for historical birth, marriage and baptismal records, while archives in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have reported significant backlogs.

The Florida connection runs deep

Canadians began arriving in Florida as early as the 1870s, drawn by work in north Florida's lumber industry and the Pensacola docks, according to the Florida Historical Quarterly. The 1925 state census counted 6,565 Canadian-born residents, then the second-largest foreign-born group in Florida after Cubans. By the 1970s and 1980s, more than a million Canadians — roughly 4% of Canada's entire population — were visiting Florida every year.

That history is still visible: a stretch of Hollywood and Hallandale Beach is known as "Little Quebec" for its concentration of French-speaking Canadian snowbirds. Seasonal numbers have dipped in 2025 amid escalating Canada-US trade tensions, but the century and a half of family ties remains.

Diaspora angle

The law matters well beyond Florida. Indian-American families with Canadian roots — and there are many, given decades of migration between India, Canada and the US — may hold the same hidden citizenship. The payoff is concrete: a Canadian passport that now ranks above the US passport on the Henley Passport Index, plus the right to live, work and vote in Canada. For families weighing a "Plan B" in an uncertain immigration climate, discovering an existing citizenship is far simpler than any visa route.

What's next

The biggest hurdle is documentation, not eligibility. Applicants must establish the chain of descent generation by generation with records from original sources — birth certificates, marriage certificates and, for older generations, baptismal or immigration records. With archives swamped, immigration lawyers recommend starting record requests early and keeping a simple family-tree diagram to map the chain. Applications show no sign of slowing, and processing times are likely to remain elevated through 2026.
